en: Preface to the *Kezhuan’an Cāolù* (A Record from the Bamboo Pavilion Hermitage). This *Cāolù* compiled by Master Guàn of Zhū’ān of the Song dynasty has long been rare in these parts.
Recently, I obtained an ancient printed edition of it at the Bàyìng Chan Monastery in Luòbèi and wished to have it carved onto woodblocks to widely benefit my fellow practitioners.

I have supplemented this with annotations in the vernacular and entrusted it to the carvers; however, I regret that the beginning is worm-eaten and destroyed over one sheet, and two characters are missing from another.
It would be a blessing if future readers could seek out superior editions to collate and restore this complete work.
Written by the Bodhisattva Śrāmaṇera Kōken during the latter part of the eleventh month in the fourth year of the Genroku era.

Additions and Appendices.

The Correct Designations for the Three Fruits of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*; Compiled by Zhuan’an. End of Table of Contents.
The meaning of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is that the mind has no place of abiding or attachment; one completely relinquishes all things, as none can be apprehended.

Thereafter, it reveals the Dharma upon which the six perfections and ten thousand practices depend: this does not go beyond the objects of the six sense-fields encountered by the six sense organs, taking these as its basis.
Regarding the deluded mind within Perfect Enlightenment, it is said: "If this deluded mind did not exist, there would be no [six sense-objects].

For those seeking merit and virtue according to the capacities of the times, the Buddha taught that such merit and virtue are like empty space. Examining this carefully according to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the Buddha stated:
"Delusion and falsehood give rise to empty space; based on empty space, the world is established. It further says: "Empty space arises within Great Awakening, like [waves] arising from the ocean."
A single bubble arises; thus, how could empty space suffice as a metaphor for the purity of the merit of *prajñā*? This also has two meanings:
first, generally, all metaphors are employed to make the difficult easy to understand and the distant manifest through the near, because among worldly things, nothing is as vast as empty space;
second, the nature of empty space is unobstructed, yet that nature cannot be apprehended. Furthermore...
The nature of space is all-pervasive, just as the Great Nirvana is used as a metaphor for the Buddha-nature pervading all places;
it is an error to mistakenly identify the manifest color-form as space. As the Sūtra says, the Buddha told Subhūti:
"All marks that exist are entirely false and illusory. This was because he had previously dispelled attachment to the marks of the Buddha’s body. Thus, regarding the bodies of the Buddhas—
If these marks are not produced by pure meritorious karma, how can they all likewise be false?
One should contemplate that the Buddha’s body has already transcended falsehood, just as one who has lost their sight does not see the sunlight—the fault lies with the seer.

If one grasps at them with attachment, there is nothing that is not false. As in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* assembly, when [the Buddha] exhorted Ānanda to return to the presence of the Buddha, the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Ānanda, when you first resolved to seek enlightenment, what superior sign did you perceive within my Dharma that caused you to suddenly renounce the world?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha: "I saw the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks, which were supremely wonderful and peerless—a mass of purple-gold light.
Because of this, I yearned for the Buddha and shaved my head to become a monk. It was simply because I perceived the Buddha’s physical marks as truly existent, not as something unreal."
The reason delusion is used to shatter attachment is that when one investigates the perceived mind across the seven locations, it is ultimately ungraspable.

Now, in this fundamental sutra, the Buddha extends the principle of the physical body to all things, showing they are universally identical to all phenomena. Once the mind arises and grasps at them, one falls into the realm of dust;
all such things are false and illusory, leaving no room for doubt. Thus, the physical marks of the Tathāgata sink into the depths of false perception.

This sutra is compiled in a single fascicle, yet throughout its upper and lower sections it frequently cites the giving of the seven treasures of a great trichiliocosm, repeatedly weighing and comparing the superiority of such merit.
People doubt this, considering it redundant and burdensome; why must it be so? Alas! When people perceive only what is near at hand, this is not to be wondered at.
However, if one speaks of the purity and vastness of Prajñā, even the great void is but a minute thing by comparison.

It also gives rise to the nature of merit, which is fundamentally inexhaustible. The Buddhas of the ten directions and the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time all employ the same perfect sound to praise it in myriad ways; even throughout vast eons, it cannot be fully reached.

In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, there are ninety chapters that repeatedly employ metaphors and comparisons. For ordinary people whose capacity for understanding has previously formed even a slight connection with this Dharma, they shall simply—
One merely looks up with faith, yet is unable to believe fully. A person from the mountains does not believe there are trees so large;
a person from the sea does not believe there are fish so large. If this is the case even regarding what is near, how much more so for what is distant?
This is why we specifically engage in such repeated weighing and comparison; herein lie two intentions: first, to accord with the capacities and conditions of beings, and second, to make them joyful.
Therefore, this single [section] serves as a guide for ordinary beings who aspire to the Buddha’s intent; their earnest devotion shall certainly not be in vain.
The ninth section, concerning the scholars of the Sūtra school, is titled here the "Chapter on the Four Fruits.

In Asaṅga’s root treatise, because the Bodhisattva on the causal stage is free from pride, although he speaks of the four fruits of the Śrāvakas, he does so to dispel attachment to the marks of realizing minor fruits and to eliminate clinging to them.
The primary purpose of this is to cause those on the stage of faith and understanding (*śraddhādhimukti-bhūmi*) to abandon their pride (*asmimāna*).

As for the śrāvaka of limited capacity who was converted by the Buddha at the Deer Park, having attained the small fruit and believing that what was to be done was already accomplished, he was subsequently rebuked and admonished throughout the various assemblies of the Vaipulya sūtras.
Thus, by the time he reached the Prajñāpāramitā assembly, he had heard extensively of the Mahāyāna.

The gates are integrated; those who cling to the Lesser Vehicle and follow their immediate inclinations—such as Subhūti, who, through the Buddha’s empowerment, has integrated all dharmas—are thus able to refrain from the thought that they have personally attained a fruit.

If even a śrāvaka of such limited capacity can achieve such faith and understanding, then those on the stages of practice will naturally transcend the notion of "I" and enter the high station of the pure mind.
In this sutra, Subhūti asks two successive questions regarding how to settle and subdue the mind. At the beginning of the discourse, he asks:
"How should one dwell? How should one subdue the mind? At the end of the discourse, he asks: "How should one dwell? How should one subdue the mind?
The former constitutes the initial inquiry, while the Buddha’s response occurs precisely in the third and fourth [chapters].
The Bodhisattva should practice the giving of alms without abiding in anything, possessing a mind of vast distribution,
a foremost mind, a constant mind, and a non-perverted mind. Later, when questioned again regarding those who are about to enter the first stage (*bhūmi*),
the Buddha replied that they merely speak of entering the stage to liberate all sentient beings, yet do not perceive any sentient beings who are liberated.
The characteristic of arising can itself ascend to a high station by abiding in Prajñā, thereby subduing and severing the root afflictions.

The meaning of the various scriptural phrases is naturally revealed; the single character "should" (應) varies in its application across the opening and middle phrases according to the intent of the sūtra.

In recent times, scholars and laypeople, not understanding the intent of the scriptures, have arbitrarily altered them—this is incorrect. One must rely on the translations of Kumārajīva from the Great Canon.
The sutra itself does not allow for its ancient course to be disturbed by shallow views.
In the seventeenth chapter, the Buddha suddenly turns his attention to address Subhūti, saying: "For example, it is like a human body that has grown large.

Thus we know that it is not only the divine mantras spoken in all the Great Teachings that are called "esoteric words" (*guhyavākya*) because they cannot be translated; rather, [this applies more broadly].
Even this single phrase in the Exoteric Teachings is itself profound and esoteric. Why?
Because this one phrase exhaustively explains how all the great Bodhisattvas enter the stage of non-arising, partially realize the Dharma-body, and fully manifest the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom;

it describes how they give rise to the great function of the Dharma-body, responding to all needs without exception and manifesting all manner of bodies, as described in the Lotus Sūtra regarding the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara.

Avalokiteśvara universally manifests form-bodies, just as in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, upon entering the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*), one enters into effortless action (*anābhoga*) and assumes ten kinds of bodies.
Not only is the primary retribution [the body] thus manifested, but the land upon which it relies is likewise nothing other than a great function.

Because Subhūti, through the power of the Buddha’s empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), was able to comprehend and integrate these teachings, and because he had eliminated all attachment to the marks of great function, the Buddha said: "The Tathāgata speaks of the human body."
When it grows large, it is not that there is a "large body"; this is called the "Great Body" because it has no place of birth.
Although people may give rise to great functions, they do not move from the body of the Dharma-nature; its greatness is due to the wondrous power of non-action.
As the preceding sutra says, for example, like Sumeru, the King of Mountains: if one relies on the eighteen abodes, this is taking the greatest body within the desire realm.

To shatter the ordinary person's grasping at signs and attachment: if one relies on Vasubandhu’s original treatise, it takes the pure lands of the Buddhas as an analogy for manifesting a body of great height;
the intent of the sutra is manifold, and one must understand it according to the capacities of beings, rather than making a unilateral determination.
The eighteenth section, the "Chapter on the Five Eyes" as expounded by the School of Exegesis, states: Ordinary beings possess the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*);
Śrāvakas cultivate and develop the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) and the wisdom eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*); and when Bodhisattvas discern all phenomena, this is called the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*).
These are all partial and shallow, unable to be fully perfected. While various sūtras and śāstras provide different analyses of these distinctions, in this sūtra, the Buddha asks Subhūti:
The Buddha, who possesses the five eyes of enlightenment, asked himself about them and stated that each exists; as he answered them one by one, he likewise stated that each exists. Some may ask:
"Why does this sutra refute [the notion of existence] while stating that each of the five eyes exists?
This "existence" is not a substantial, grasped entity; it is merely designated as "existing. This is to demonstrate that the Buddha-eye shines universally, lacking nothing.

This is because the Dharma-realm is thoroughly penetrated and there is nothing that is not seen. Next, the scriptural text reveals that the Buddha’s wisdom is perfectly luminous and there is nothing it does not know;
yet this "thorough knowledge" arises because all minds are found to be ungraspable and the limits of the three periods of time are severed.
Thus, he is able to be unimpeded and is able to fully know all differentiated minds and mental factors. This constitutes the ten titles of the Buddha.

He is named the Perfectly All-Knowing One (*Samyaksaṃbuddha*). The karmic activities of ordinary beings are exhausted, and they fully manifest the Buddha-mind, as extensively described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*;
I shall not cite it here at length. The twenty-first section of the sutra is incorporated into a separate translation consisting of sixty-two characters, following the version by Asaṅga.
According to this passage, the Buddha-mind is complete; first, Subhūti takes sentient beings as the object of the Buddha-mind’s contemplation.
Question: Will there be those who, hearing this Dharma taught in future ages, give rise to faith?

If one were to pose this same question based on the preceding sutra passage—asking whether there might be those who, upon hearing it, give rise to true faith—the Buddha answered that in the final five hundred years they would be able to give rise to faith and take this as reality.
Now, since the question here is the same as before, why does the Buddha answer by saying, "They are not among the assembly"?
Birth is not non-being; one must know that this is the profound and subtle interplay between the capacity [of the disciple] and the response [of the Buddha].
Although this is similar to what was asked previously, the intent of this present question is to demonstrate that the Buddha-mind is ultimately pure, like a great round mirror.
Regarding the state of mind first aroused therein, although it is fundamentally for the sake of sentient beings, one realizes that all sentient beings are ungraspable.
The Buddha’s mind and the realm of sentient beings—what distinction can there be between mind and realm? All natures are empty; yet this emptiness is not annihilation. Therefore it is said:
"They are not sentient beings, nor are they not sentient beings. To say they are not sentient beings is precisely what is called being sentient beings.

Kumārajīva’s translation abbreviates this because, from the initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) through the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), these are already the objects of the Buddha-mind’s contemplation; thus, as previously noted, [the text] has already addressed this.
This has been stated briefly.

The ultimate essence of this sutra lies solely in the departure from signs (*lakṣaṇa*); because the Buddhas have no other extraordinary distinction beyond this, it is said that "departing from all signs is what constitutes the Buddhas.
The root of the illnesses of sentient beings is simply attachment to signs; as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "But..."
It removes the illness but does not remove the Dharma; this is because prior to this, one was detached from attachment to the marks of the Buddha’s form-body (*rūpakāya*).

Therefore, it says "seeing" [the second division], which is for the purpose of detaching from attachment to the marks of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Thus, it says "contemplating the external marks of the form-body.

The Dharma-body is the internal essence, while the form-body is the external mark. Although the causes—the hundred merits—are complete, the Dharma-body manifests; yet, if one sees only the external marks...
Since there is nothing that is not the internal essence, it is said that one contemplates the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks;
yet, fearing that one might still cling to external characteristics as the Dharma-body Buddha, [the Buddha] further cites that even a Cakravartin King possesses such marks of merit.

Although he possesses seven matters, he does not equal the Buddha. Since the external marks are similar, this recourse to a worldly matter serves to shatter attachment, thereby causing one to contemplate the Dharma-body directly.

Because the internal essence is both identical and yet distinct, it is said that [the dharmas] should not be [grasped as such]. The physical forms and voices of the Buddhas are none other than the Dharma-body;
yet, if one takes them as objects of attachment, they are all non-existent.
Nāgārjuna composed the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* in one hundred fascicles to explain the thirty fascicles of the *Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, totaling nine [volumes].

The ten chapters of this sutra extensively discourse upon the single character "Tathā" (如). "Tathā" takes non-movement as its meaning; it is the ultimate principle of the Prajñāpāramitā, being simply "Suchness" (如如).
Since the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is fundamentally unmoving, this sutra states: "The Tathāgata is the meaning of the Suchness of all dharmas.
When all things are merged into a single essence without any differentiation, one realizes that all Buddhas of the ten directions arise from this.
Coming from the meaning of "suchness" (tathatā) and departing into the meaning of "suchness," there is nowhere from which one comes and nowhere to which one goes;

yet the Ten Epithets specifically name him "Tathāgata" (Thus-Come One) to accord with worldly convention. In reality, both persons and phenomena are all suchness; therefore, the end of the sutra says:
"Do not grasp at signs; remain unmoving in suchness. Suchness has no basis of reliance, for it is like the great void, and the void has nothing upon which to rely.
As Ratnākara praised the Buddha for penetrating the characteristics of all phenomena without obstruction, he prostrated himself before the One who is like space,

having no dependence. How could one who perceives false views and discriminates various distinctions among all phenomena be unobstructed as they flow through birth and death toward the boundless future?
Regarding these thirty-two sections of this sutra, it is traditionally said that Prince Zhaoming of the Liang Dynasty established these divisions and assigned them their names.

It is certain that the original compilation contained these section titles; some correspond to the titles in Asaṅga’s *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Root Verses), while others differ entirely.

The established section titles mostly follow what is explained in the sutra itself. However, if one wishes to exhaustively establish the underlying principles, one must rely upon the original treatise. I. [End of Section]
The eighteenth dwelling finally reveals the intent of the sutra. As for the thirty-two sections, how can they be called "manifestations of transformation rather than the real"?
This has been briefly addressed in the *Shiyuan* (Garden of Meanings), where it was suggested that the names of this section and the fifth section should be exchanged.
At the end of the sutra, this section’s commentary by Asaṅga states: "How does one expound it for others? Without grasping at marks, in accordance with suchness."
The first four lines [of the verse] concern being unstained while preaching the Dharma; the final four lines concern being unstained while transmigrating.
However, after the statement on being unstained while preaching the Dharma, the subsequent question "Why is this so? (*tat kasya hetoḥ*) serves as a term for inquiry and explanation.

Once the inquiry and explanation are established, there are these four lines. How could they pertain to being unstained while transmigrating? The entire passage of the scripture is not at all related to that; it is solely for this reason.
The meaning of the Sūtra is profound and subtle, and furthermore, the translators favored a style that was concise and archaic. For what reason, then, would there be two different interpretations?

If one explains it from the perspective of the Dharma being preached, and subsequently considers the person who receives it—the capacity of the recipient and the response of the teaching—then even if one grasps at appearances, everything is nothing but the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), like a dream or an illusion; how much more so for ordinary beings who are currently caught in the cycle of transmigration?

Therefore it is said that there is nothing this scripture does not encompass. Had it not been for Asaṅga’s personal vision [of Maitreya], no teacher of the world in future ages could have reached such a level.
For sixty years I have studied this scripture; though I regret my inability to bring forth any profound illumination, I have merely sought out its phrases and meanings.

Apart from the two works, the *Shiyuan tonglun* (Comprehensive Discussion of the Garden of Meanings) and the *Tonglun* (Comprehensive Discussion), I have occasionally gathered [notes] following the text as they occurred. Furthermore, I have also reached [this point].
These twelve chapters comprise my life’s work as I approach eighty-five years of age; being but a man at the twilight of his days, I have composed these as a final gift of Dharma.
Drafted on the Mid-Autumn Festival of the Bingshen year of the Chunxi era.
In response to the ten questions posed by Zisanda, it is asked:
All the great teachings extensively discuss the phenomena of the ten directions and the three periods of time as being interrelated; they do not transcend these spatial and temporal dimensions.
Why, then, does the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* refer to the ten directions as the "ten voids," while the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* refers to the three periods of time as the "three limits"?

Regarding the meanings of "direction" (*diś*) and "limit" (*anta*) as applied to the world (*loka*), what are they? It may be said that the spatial dimensions of the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) can be termed "direction" and "limit.

Answer: Spatial dimensions have specific referents, while the world must be continuous; since spatial dimensions and the world intersect, there is no principle for abandoning one in favor of the other, as in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
The profound teaching of transformation unfolds in three layers—ten, hundred, and thousand—pervading the ten directions without obstruction within the void.
Thus, the ten directions are termed the "ten voids. Because the three periods of time continue in succession without interruption, the three times are termed the "three limits" (*jì*);
to speak of "limits" is to imply the "limitless," for the meaning lies beyond the words. This is the *Prajñāpāramitā*’s forty-two characters.
The mentalities of those in the Hīnayāna are all like this: their measures are limited, and they fixate upon names and characteristics.
Question: All the Mahāyāna teachings extensively discuss the world, the kalpas, and sentient beings—these three are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and must therefore have an end.
For what reason does the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra state in all cases that they are inexhaustible?

Answer: Regarding the kalpas and numbers of worlds and sentient beings, if they were something produced through volitional thought arising from the mind, they would be conditioned, finite, and possessable in form and number;
however, because the nature of the dharma-realm pervades all three [worlds, kalpas, and beings] and is inexhaustible by nature, the dharmas are also inexhaustible.
Question: Since all great teachings are *sūtras*, why is it that only the *Avataṃsaka* is said to have "retinues"?
Answer: The term *sūtra* is a general designation in Sanskrit for both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings; its direct translation is "Scripture of Accordance with Reality" (*Kyi-kyong*).

However, regarding the specific intent of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it elucidates the ocean of nature (*dharmatā-samudra*) and universally encompasses all as its primary root text, while all others are its retinues. Why is this so?

However, throughout the various sutras, the Flower Garland (Avataṃsaka) Sūtra’s ocean of nature is explained in every word and in every world-system; these explanations do not contradict the intent of the scriptures, as they universally encompass all things without exception as their retinue.

Question: Regarding the circulation of the "Entering the Dharma Realm" (Jingjie pin) chapter at the end of the Flower Garland Sūtra, some accounts state that it exists while others state that it does not. Master Qingliang [Chengguan] has addressed this concurrently...
As for whether this accords with the intent of the sutra or not:

the answer is that the "Heavenly Canopy" (Mitiān) high judgment accords with the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*. Regarding the various schools' methods of interpreting the sutras, it is necessary to divide them into three parts;

while the sectional divisions of most sutras make their circulation somewhat easier, regarding the *Avataṃsaka*, ancient masters mostly maintained that one portion should be divided from the end of the sutra.

A verse states: "Some may say that the inexhaustible and cool nature of the Dharma-realm encompasses both merit and function; yet, fearing this may lead to ambiguity, how is it better than directly taking Master Guangtong?
For in the 'Entering the Dharma-realm' chapter, there is nothing that does not circulate the ocean-nature of the Dharma-realm;

its circulation is inexhaustible, as Sudhana’s universal pilgrimage continues until the end of the future. When comparing the beginning and end of this Sutra of Many Merits, what has been proclaimed previously [is confirmed]."
It is not necessary for the Buddha himself to circulate the sutras at their conclusion; rather, the compilers of the scriptures simply summarize what has been previously taught.

Question: All great teachings expound upon cause and effect—whether through the exposition of the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, the two dharmas of cause and effect, or various incidental explanations, or by speaking specifically of causes or of effects. Why is this so?
Only for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* must one explain the "ten suchnesses. Jingxi said: "The ten suchnesses are simply the natural law (*dharmatā*) of cause and effect.
Answer: There is a saying of former worthies: "That which the successive sages have discussed reaches its ultimate in the Buddha, because his Buddha-dharma is unsurpassed."
There is nothing that can surpass this ultimate realization of non-attainment; it is the fundamental principle that elucidates cause and effect, transcending all else.

Therefore, it resides solely in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, where it is explained through the "Ten Suchnesses" as the dharma of cause and effect. This establishes the core teaching of the one sutra across its three cycles of exposition.

The opening of the provisional to reveal the true body is realized only by Buddhas and Buddhas throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time—the ultimate, final, and most profound depth.
Because the spheres of experience are all-pervasive, the ultimate discourse on cause and effect speaks of the "ten suchnesses.
The Great Master Tiantai’s *Mohe Zhiguan* points to this as the source of the wondrous object; Jingxi [Zhiyi] indicated this to the students so that they might understand it thoroughly.

Question: Since the "opening of the original ground" (*mūla-vivaraṇa*) in the *Lotus Sūtra* pertains to Śākyamuni’s long-standing attainment of Buddhahood, how does it relate to the present-day śrāvakas entering the Mahāyāna, which necessarily requires the opening of the original ground?
Answer: The *Lotus Sūtra* reveals that Śākyamuni’s original ground was attained as a Buddha long ago; therefore, it is necessary to open this original ground.
As for the śrāvakas, although they have entered the Great Vehicle, they still cling to their former traces;

thus, for them, it is necessary to reveal the original ground. Furthermore, since these śrāvakas have already entered the Great Vehicle and attained the first stage of the Perfect Teaching (the First Abode), they must further progress through subsequent stages to increase their Path and diminish their births. This is especially so for those of the Perfect nature who have entered the stage of non-arising.
Flowing in spontaneously, it is intended solely for Śrāvakas to enter through the gate of giving.
Question: Tiantai established four teachings—Zang, Tong, Bie, and Yuan—to explain the meanings of all sutras across the five periods of one Buddha’s transformation;
Xianshou established five teachings—the initial and final Small Vehicle, and the Sudden and Complete—wherein the two schools differ in their names and definitions of the teachings.
Question: Regarding these slight differences, how do the fundamental application and the ultimate destination differ?
Answer: Tiantai established the names and meanings of the teachings; however, it was only the Great Master of Tiantai who definitively determined the fundamental names of the teachings.

While the ultimate goal of the Buddha-dharma is the single, true principle (*ekayāna-tattva*), the capacities of sentient beings were not yet ready to receive [the teaching] directly from that single, true principle. Therefore, he provisionally applied [the teachings] accordingly.

The gate through which one emerges from provisional principles and enters ultimate principle is called "Teaching" (*śāsana*). Teaching must correspond to the spiritual capacity (*indriya*) of the recipient;

as these capacities vary between sharp and dull, the approach taken differs accordingly. Thus, there are only four [approaches]: first, the transformation through the Five Periods, which is the method employed according to the time, with variations in its application and extent.
One must interpret the meaning according to the teaching without deviating from the established track, until finally reaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, where the provisional is opened.

They all ultimately converge upon the single reality. Although Xianshou established his teachings according to what was stated in the sutras—seeing only the branches and leaves rather than inferring the fundamental root—the general consensus of the teaching schools did not dare arbitrarily adopt them as their primary authority. Qingliang harmonized these views, taking principle as the foundation of his teaching.
Question: When Dharmakṣema translated the six-fascicle *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, it was stated that icchantikas lack Buddha-nature.

When Zhu Daosheng strove to defend this principle, his contemporaries did not believe him. However, when the original version of the sutra arrived, it was indeed stated that all icchantikas possess Buddha-nature.
From this point on, although people knew that all icchantikas possess Buddha-nature, they still did not believe that insentient things also possess Buddha-nature.

Regarding the force with which Jingxi’s *Jinbi* (The Golden Scalpel) attempts to rescue this doctrine—whether one asserts that insentient things possess Buddha-nature or denies it—where does the fundamental gain or loss lie? Answer:

Jingxi’s *Jinbi* was intended to protect the sentiments of the time; he did not wish to directly refute [the opposing view], but merely stated that there are those who cite the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* divides *tathatā* into two categories: that which resides in sentient beings is called "Buddha-nature" (*buddhadhātu*), and that which resides in insentient things is called "Dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*).
However, Jingxi [Zhiyi] personally read and meticulously examined the treatise and found no such statement therein;

he verified this against the sutras and śāstras and concluded that in all the great teachings, Buddha-nature and Dharma-nature are merely different names for the same reality. Alas! If [this were the view of] Zhu Daosheng...
While this Elder was alive, there was no need for further blades; students must know that he taught that insentient things possess Buddha-nature.

This realization depends upon the Great Teaching of the Mind-Only, wherein all phenomena are identical in essence and all natures are pervasive. To say that insentient things lack Buddha-nature is to lose it;
one can see that the fundamental difference between gaining and losing this truth is more than just the distance between heaven and abyss.

Question: Although there are those who believe that insentient things possess Buddha-nature, there is still debate regarding this. If insentient things do indeed possess Buddha-nature, how could they preach the Dharma?
Among the ancient worthies, some pointed to a tree and spoke of suffering and emptiness, or pointed to a mote of dust and spoke of lands;
is this considered reasonable or unreasonable?
Answer: If one has already gained faith in the principle that insentient things possess Buddha-nature, one must necessarily advance to a state where fundamental non-discrimination is realized.
Once you ask whether insentient things, having Buddha-nature, can also preach the Dharma, you have already fallen into discrimination. Not only do insentient things lack it;
even so-called sentient beings likewise lack Buddha-nature, being nothing more than the proliferating karmic consciousnesses of sentient beings.

Question: Regarding the Buddha-nature of insentient beings, the Tiantai school’s traditional teachings have only ever focused on interpreting the *Jingxi Jibei* (The Golden Scalpel) and the *Fuxing Zhuanji* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), yet it is not known in which specific text of Tiantai Master [Zhiyi] this doctrine was originally expounded.
Answer: Jingxi [Zhiyi], entrusting his views to a guest through a dream, specially composed the *Jinbi* (The Golden Scalpel) to establish that the Great Teaching holds that "all is but mind.

In the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), he established ten meanings as scriptural citations for the *Mohe Zhiguan*, stating that "not a single color or fragrance is not the Middle Way Buddha-nature," and that this nature pervades all colors, fragrances, and even insentient phenomena. Yet, why did the Great Master Tiantai... [text ends]...?
However, these passages from the Shanjia (Mountain School) teachings on the perfect discourse of the inherent nature are all such texts.

The Tiantai school, as a lineage of Nāgārjuna’s Dharma-nature tradition, has grasped the essential meaning and thus takes the doctrine of the inherent nature as its core; to study the Tiantai teachings, one must possess the "eye of the school."
In the Tiantai school, which upholds the Great Teaching of Mind-Only, the lineage of succession reached the ninth patriarch, the Venerable Jingxi.

His merit lay in recording the profound intent of the Perfect School (Yuanzong) of the Buddha Vehicle through written texts, exerting great effort to rescue the doctrine that insentient beings possess Buddha-nature; for if one were to say that insentient beings lack it...
If one says there is "nature" (*xing*), then it would not be appropriate to say there are "insentient things. This is the general conclusion.

In my book *The Golden Scalpel* (*Jinbi*), written as a temporary lodging for a dream, I have stated: "If one does not realize that the mind alone is the essence that possesses all things, then all the Great Teachings will be entirely useless.
From this, one knows that all the Great Teachings universally take "mind-only" (*weixin*) as their fundamental principle.
It should be specifically understood that in the *Avataṃsaka*, one should contemplate the nature of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) as being entirely created by mind alone.

This sutra takes the dharma-realm as its essence, "mind-only" as its central tenet, and universal inclusion as its function. Since all phenomena are identical in essence and pervasive in nature, why restrict the statement to "mind-only"?
This is because it accords with delusion; since the mind is the root of affliction, and proceeding from what is proximate and essential, it is said to be "mind-only. Thus, it is opened up.

The principle of this meaning is that all phenomena (*dharmas*), every single one, are exclusively [mind] and have nothing external. To take even a single phenomenon as an example, all phenomena are without anything external;
all are exclusively [mind]. This is precisely what the Great Master Tiantai meant by the "Perfect Four Mindfulnesses":

exclusively form, exclusively sound, exclusively fragrance, exclusively taste, exclusively touch, and exclusively mental objects (*dharma*). These six sense-objects are all exclusively [mind], with none left uncaptured. Furthermore, as for the subject...

Only non-existence cannot create [anything]. Why? It is because the nature of all phenomena is fundamentally identical; as soon as one engages in conceptual deliberation, it becomes a superfluous dharma, and the meaning of "only" is not established.
One must simply perform analysis until even the finest details are completely swept away. This is what the Great Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra by the Great Sage Nāgārjuna meant when he said:
"Where the movements of the mind cease and the path of language is cut off, the conventional expressions of the world cannot reach the ultimate truth."
The eye of the teachings must not fail to be clear; if there are divergent views, they are the work of Māra Pāpīyas. I send this message to future students: you must find true teachers and friends.
This humble old man, without considering his own limitations, has reached this point; it is only I, of Siming, who have attained self-realization through mental contemplation.
The *Lotus Sūtra* reveals the provisional teachings;
the Great Master Tiantai manifested in the body of a bhikṣu, attained awakening at Dàsù, and practiced the Way at Tiantai.

With a heart of great compassion, he mastered the sūtras and śāstras, returned to the essential source of the *Lotus Sūtra*, and grasped the Buddha’s transformative intent. Thus, the teaching was transmitted through Jiangzhe for over a hundred years.

At this grand assembly, we are about to lecture on the *Fahua Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra) and the *Fahua Wenju* (Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sūtra). Whenever we encounter the "opening of the provisional" (*kaishen*), we must raise questions:
Is the provisional being opened that which is of the same substance (*tongti*) as the real? Or is it the provisional of a different substance (*yiti*)?

If it is the opening of the provisional of a different substance, why does the *Xuanyi*, in its explanation of the general title of the sūtra, employ the three analogies of the lotus flower to represent the Wondrous Dharma (*miaofa*) all together? If it is the opening of the provisional of the same substance, why [does the *Wenju* state] regarding the *Lotus Sūtra*...

Regarding the textual explanations, the titles of the chapters, the skillful means (*upāya*), and the functional applications of the Dharma, these have historically belonged to distinct entities that were opened up [for exposition].
When questioned as to what constitutes this "opening," it is said that the three provisional means are identical to the one ultimate reality.

Those of initial capacity who wander in study merely gaze upon them with admiration; they dare not venture a single word to participate in the deliberations of the assembly. As for me, of humble years, I have only recently reached twenty.
On the final day, I reflected that all previous deliberations were not a thorough examination of the *Lotus Sūtra*’s true doctrine.

Since the provisional teachings have already been revealed as being inherently wondrous, and the Buddha has already earnestly praised the skillful means (*upāya*), what need is there to ask whether the three formal assemblies (*trikoṭika*) concern the revelation of the same essence (*tongti*) or different essences (*yiti*)?
Whether one adheres to one side or subsumes both the same and different, the provisional is itself...

This truly belongs to the revelation of the ultimate meaning (*nītārtha*) and does not concern the disclosure of the provisional (*neyārtha*). This [interpretation] erroneously treats the revelation of the ultimate as the disclosure of the provisional;
it fails to recognize that the aforementioned passage in the original sūtra refers to this very sūtra’s opening of the gate of skillful means (*upāyamukha*).

What the sūtra means by "opening the gate of skillful means" is that the Buddha, through the power of his skillful means, manifested the teachings of the three vehicles (*triyāna*); this constitutes the main text of the brief opening of the provisional in this sūtra. The term "śrāvaka" (voice-hearer) refers to those who are near [to the goal].

This means that the exhaustion of emotional afflictions (*kleśa*) depends upon this scripture; the title "Wondrous Dharma" (*Saddharma-puṇḍarīka-sūtra*) and its chapter headings signify that the provisional (*upāya*) is already wondrous within the fundamental reality (*mūla-tattva*), and thus there is no contradiction.

As soon as one engages with it, it is the Real (*bhūta*); it is not a case of opening up the provisional (*apāvṛtyopāya*). If one were to distinguish the provisional and the real as having different essences (*nānātva-svabhāva*), such a judgment would be like the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation), which universally lists the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*)—the three categories (*tri-koṭi*)—under the objective realm of the aggregates (*skandha-viṣaya*).
If one wishes to employ the mind for contemplation, one must necessarily select the *vijñāna-skandha* (the aggregate of consciousness) as the essential substance of the object of observation.

How could the Great Master Tiantai have ever uttered a single word regarding the three minds of the indeterminate, the wholesome, or the unwholesome? These three belong to the mental characteristics (*citta-nimitta*) that arise from and are objects of the *vijñāna-skandha*;
they are not the essential substance of the creating mind itself. Even those who lecture on the teachings persist in disputing whether one may contemplate all three.
To contemplate the indeterminate with a distracted mind is a waste of words; fundamentally, there is no such thing. One sees here the saying of the sages of old:

"The world is fundamentally without affairs. This has been realized now. In years past, my discourse on the High Seat was not lacking in clarity, yet I still feared that its transmission might not have reached a state of intimate realization.
With few days remaining, I have arrived at this point through my humble efforts.
Regarding the discernment of the objects of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, a verse from the *Mahā-śāstra* states: "Within all worlds, nothing exists beyond name and form (*nāma-rūpa*).
If one wishes to contemplate according to reality, one should contemplate only name and form. The true mind cannot be apprehended, and the deluded mind cannot be seen; there is only name. Name is..."
Regarding the mind, Master Tiantai taught that the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) establishes the objects of contemplation for practitioners at the initial stage.

These encompass the five aggregates (*skandha*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and eighteen elements (*dhātu*)—the three categories of all phenomena comprising both form and mind—which correspond to the gateways to enlightenment through the "perfect penetration" of the twenty-five sages in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
However, for a practitioner at the initial stage, these are too broad and diffuse to be easily employed as objects of contemplation.

One must necessarily select [the primary element], just as one discards the *zhang* to take the *chi*, or discards the *chi* to take the *cun*. This serves as an analogy for selecting the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) from among the phenomena currently manifesting;
the mind-factor of the consciousness-aggregate, which has been the creator of all dharmas throughout beginningless daily life, is the object of observation.

As for the three types of mind—neutral, wholesome, and unwholesome—they belong to the mental states that arise; they are not the creative essence of the mind and are therefore not the objects to be selected.

The *Liyuan duijing suiziyi samādhi* (Samādhi of Following One’s Own Intent Amidst Circumstances and Objects) is precisely the essential object of contemplation (*guan-jing*). One must know that practicing contemplation necessarily requires discernment.
Jingxi [Zhiyi] said: "Regarding 'the indeterminate,' this refers generally to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Since matter and mind belong to the aggregate of retribution (*vipāka-skandha*), when contrasted with the nine objects of affliction (*kleśa*) that arise below, they are distinguished as either non-virtuous or evil to delineate the three minds; thus, the fundamental distinction is inherently clear."

It was not difficult to see from the beginning that it is a pity that Dharma Master Nanping Zhen, who once proclaimed the Way and presided over the Dharma as a man of wisdom of his time, did not know why he confusedly spoke of the "three minds.
Since then, this has been inherited: some observe the three minds collectively, while others observe the indeterminate mind separately.
Furthermore, there are those who delight in eccentricity and arbitrarily create doctrinal categories, leading to such confusion. What is the point of this? I heard this many years ago.

Furthermore, when one has something under one's own charge, one should speak thus to one's fellow students; yet, fearing that it might be transmitted erroneously, I dwell in leisure and inaction, following directly what is correct.
Why must one minutely examine and verify each point? Contemplation and cessation (śamatha-vipaśyanā) are as clear as pointing at something with one’s fingers.
Regarding the ten kinds of realms of the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra*:
formerly, while traveling and studying on Mount Xi (Xishan), I saw Master Laobi lecturing daily on the *Waidao benxing jing* at Ruike Pavilion.
He burned *agallochum* incense, the fragrance of which never ceased. One day, I adjusted my robes and went to pay my respects; I sat beside him and prostrated myself in attendance.

In the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation), Master Tiantai cites the *Puxian guan* (Contemplation of Samantabhadra) regarding the ten kinds of realms prior to the stage of non-arising (*anutpāda*).

He compiled these ten titles according to the sutra and divided the textual passages accordingly. Furthermore, because he specifically adhered to the title of the sutra as "Contemplating Samantabhadra," he established Samantabhadra as the object of contemplation for the beginner’s mind.
[The author of this commentary] earnestly and sincerely remonstrated against this view, but the Master’s intention was not changed; thus, the sub-commentary (*shu*) was completed.

Once this has been practiced, there is nothing that is not compliant. Students must know that when the Great Master Tiantai pointed to the ten kinds of states prior to the stage of non-arising (*anutpāda*) in the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-sūtra*, he did not originally intend them to divide the scripture; rather, he intended them as a general indication of the true cause of the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
This refers to the initial stage of the first resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda*), prior to the stage of non-arising, based on what is taught in this single sutra. One should recite [this] accordingly.

In the Mahāyāna sūtras, by cultivating Mahāyāna practices, one accomplishes the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) and attains a semblance of the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*), as described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

This involves the fourfold signs of realization—namely, the majesty of merit, the vision of Samantabhadra, the appearance of Prabhūtaratna, and the manifestation of the divided bodies of Śākyamuni—which are combined and indicated therein;
thus, they are termed the "ten kinds of realms. This is according to the *Fahua sanmei yi* (Ritual for the Lotus Samādhi) of the Great Master Tiantai.
Subsequently, drawing from various sutras, I have arranged the stages of shallow and deep realization and the characteristics of perfected practice regarding precept, concentration, and wisdom.

This is intended to provide comfort and encouragement by making the characteristics of these attainments clear through the sutras themselves. The sutra says: "Those who recite Mahāyāna sutras, cultivate Mahāyāna practices, and delight in beholding the form-body of Samantabhadra;
those who delight in beholding the stupa of Prabhūtaratna; and those who delight in beholding Śākyamuni Buddha and his [disciples]..."

Regarding the passage "The bodies of all Buddhas delight in attaining the purity of the six sense organs," although the phrasing appears inverted, it should be understood through the intended meaning.
If one were to list ten kinds of realms, the purity of the six sense organs would come first, followed by the four kinds of signs of realization;

for the signs of realization are attained through the power of practice. However, these realms as described in the scriptural text correspond to the various stages of cultivation throughout a single lifetime.
These do not obstruct one another in their ethical order; one must wait until the general outline is clear before they can be divided into sections.
As for the subsequent disclosure of the six faculties, they follow the sequence as explained, and all exist according to conditions within the Buddha’s intent.

The ten types specifically mention "objects" (*viṣaya*), because the Sūtra states: "First, contemplate the initial object of Samantabhadra," and also: "This is called the initial object of the eye faculty."
Because of these characteristics, one enters the stage of non-arising and flows into it spontaneously without relying on expedient means;

how could there be a sūtra title that speaks of "contemplating" when the modes of perception and vision differ? In the sixteen contemplations, the initial mind establishes objects through mental imagery (*saṃjñā*) and contemplates them;

this realization is common to the vision of all Buddhas. Mental imagery also applies to the two Great Beings, as well as the nine grades of rebirth; yet, in the title of that sūtra, it simply says: [The Sūtra of Immeasurable Life].

Regarding the term "Buddha," according to what the Great Master Tiantai meant by "the master who recounts the teachings encompassing his disciples," the title of this scripture should simply refer collectively to the one who expounds the repentance in this sutra.
As the evening sun was already pressing down, he composed this for the sake of the future, entrusting it to the leisurely seclusion of Zhuan-an.

Regarding the ten dharma-realms and the ten suchnesses, the Great Master Tiantai’s judgment and exposition of all the various scriptures of the Buddha’s teaching must examine what the scripture teaches: if the Dharma is great, it is a great Dharma;
if small, it is a small Dharma. If great, it explains a vast and expansive Dharma; if small, it explains a narrow and limited Dharma. [Vast and expansive...]

Thus, [the teachings] that exhaustively encompass the nature and characteristics of the ten dharma realms are broad, whereas those that are restricted to the six dharma realms—both the environment and its inhabitants—are narrow.

All great teachings that expound the Dharma necessarily address the ten dharma realms; although their exposition of the Dharma is universal, what is taught according to specific conditions may not be complete.

Even though the teaching is thus [partial], the Dharma itself must be universal. Only then can one know that the *Avataṃsaka*, *Vaipulya*, *Prajñāpāramitā*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and *Mahāparinirvāṇa* [sūtras] are all [inclusive].
Since all great teachings expound the principle that "all is but mind," and that which is created by mind necessarily encompasses all ten dharma-realms without exception,

the ten dharma-realms are not taught exclusively in the *Avataṃsaka*. Rather, it is because the *Avataṃsaka* subsumes all phenomena as its totality and reveals the inexhaustible nature of all dharmas,
that the transmission of the *Avataṃsaka* teaching of the ten dharma-realms has been so widespread.
In reality, the Dharma-realm is the *Avataṃsaka*; there is not a single text that fully and exhaustively enumerates it.

As for the Buddha’s praise of the "ten suchnesses" at the beginning of the "Expedient Means" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, what Jingxi [Zhiyi] called the "ten suchnesses" is simply the natural law (*dharmatā*) of cause and effect.

Furthermore, there is no great teaching among all the Mahāyāna scriptures that does not communicate this law of cause and effect; it is merely a matter of distinguishing between the general and the specific aspects of cause and effect.

It is not that [the *Lotus Sūtra*] is distinct; rather, it is because it alone reaches the ultimate consummation of all phenomena from beginning to end, extending to the "ten suchnesses," in order to praise the single true body of this entire scripture—the opening of the provisional (*upāya*) through the three assemblies—which pervades all dharmas. As the Sūtra says:
"Only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena"; subsequently, it explains and fully enumerates how all phenomena are complete.

Regarding these ten "suchnesses," I have recently heard that scholars in Eastern Zhejiang ask why the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* speaks of the ten dharma-realms while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* speaks of the ten suchnesses.

They argue that what the two sutras teach differs in its coarseness and subtlety; thus, Guifeng [Zongmi] remarked that while the *Lotus Sūtra* is rich in phrasing and vast in meaning, it truly yields to the *Avataṃsaka*.
For how can the *Avataṃsaka*, which proclaims the nature of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-svabhāva*) while expounding all phenomena, be compared to this?
How coarse it is! I fear that the younger generation of the Western Zhejiang region has not yet resolved this; even in his final years, Zhuan’an could not avoid being hasty.

Regarding the intent of establishing the teaching, I read the *New Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra* by the National Teacher Qingliang (Zongmi)—a work based on the teachings of the Tang dynasty’s Xianshou (Fazang)—during my early years. Prior to the commentary...

In this section on the principles [of doctrine], while there is no leisure to discuss the various schools' systems of teaching in their entirety, I have observed that when matching Xianshou’s Five Teachings with Tiantai’s Four Teachings—Specific, Common, Shared, and Complete—the author consistently relies upon Qingliang’s synthesis of these great teachings. Such talent and insight are truly admirable;
yet, it is a pity that in correlating the two schools’ systems of teaching, he failed to examine the specific ways in which each school established its own doctrinal framework.
One should observe that Xianshou’s Five Teachings were established merely according to what was stated in the various sutras to serve as a framework for interpreting those schools;
thus, scholars of those traditions have criticized Tiantai’s fixed "Five Periods" classification of the scriptures.

As for the Four Teachings of Transformation and Dharma established by Tiantai, these were not created by the Buddha either, because the nature of the Dharma is such and because the capacities of sentient beings differ. Thus, the teachings [arise].
In this way, the principle elucidated by the teaching and the ultimate principle reached through practice constitute the Middle Way as the true principle;

the provisional principle of true emptiness is established for those whose capacities and desires seek the principle, which must necessarily proceed through teaching and practice. Because those with the capacity for the true principle of the Middle Way have sharp faculties, they realize that the environment they encounter is immediately the Middle Way, and there is nothing that is not truly real;
thus, the Perfect Teaching (Enkyō) is established. If, however, the capacity is dull, one must rely on gradual expedient means.

The Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) is established for those with sharp faculties regarding the provisional principle of true emptiness; therefore, it is taught that all phenomena are illusory existence, which is itself emptiness.
The Shared Teaching (Tong-jiao) is established because this teaching is not only common to the Three Vehicles, but also allows for entry into the Separate and Complete Teachings;

however, as the faculties of those regarding the provisional principle of true emptiness are dull, it is taught that the causes and effects of the triple world are substantially real, and one must sever the afflictions of view and thought.
The establishment of the Tripiṭaka Teaching is based on the notion that afflictions give rise to *paricchinna-janma-śarīra* (segmented birth-and-death).

Therefore, this teaching takes the "Peaceful Practices" (*anurakṣaṇā-caryā*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as its standard for the *sthiti* (establishment) period, while it excludes the *pravartana* (circulation) period by using the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* to disparage the Lesser Vehicle.

It is specifically termed "Tripiṭaka" to manifest that this particular teaching is not comprehensive or integrated. Within the capacity of the Buddha's single transformation, there are the sudden and the gradual, the secret and the indeterminate.

It is solely because their capacities differ. If it were otherwise, for those of the single class of the Hīnayāna Śrāvakas within the Tripiṭaka, whose root-natures must necessarily be transformed through a gradual process—being matured over five periods before being brought together in a single moment at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*—there would still remain residual capacities that await the manifestation of their nature in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.
Thus, there is no difference in their ultimate return to the perfect, secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa*) of the letter "I" (the *E* of *ekayāna*).

Reaching the ultimate consummation, the scale of Tiantai’s establishment of the teachings is vast and great. The Buddhas of the ten directions and the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time share one and the same perfect sound, like a pearl rolling upon a platter.
The Great Master of Tiantai attained awakening and profound penetration, moving as freely as the wind through space; even their praises could not suffice.

Having encountered this flourishing dynasty, he ordained a great number of monks; I have briefly recorded these circumstances for the sake of establishing karmic connections for those who may travel and study hereafter.
In producing this work, it must be written in plain and accessible prose; this may suffice for one to gain a rough understanding of its general framework.

Regarding the title of the Tripiṭaka teachings, the *Mahā-śāstra* in one hundred fascicles, which provides a literary commentary on the ninety chapters of the sutras, concludes with the statement: "When the Buddha was in the world, there were no [Tripiṭakas]."
In the Tibetan tradition, there are only the names "Bhikṣu who upholds the Sūtras," "Bhikṣu who upholds the Vinaya," and "Bhikṣu who upholds the Mātṛkā.

However, while the Buddha was in the world, there were no such designations for the Three Piṭakas. For what reason, then, does the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (The Lotus Sutra), in its "Peaceful Practices" chapter, speak of those who are attached to the Small Vehicle and study the Three Piṭakas?
Both this sutra and this treatise were translated by Master Kumārajīva; some have explained them as being consistent [with the original].
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the Three Piṭakas were first divided prior to the compilation (*saṃgīti*) and after the compilation. Now, I ask:

does the *Anraku-gyō* (Peaceful Conduct) chapter of the Lotus Sūtra belong to the period after the compilation? To begin with, the Great Master Tiantai established the four teachings of transformation; he designated the one teaching of the Hīnayāna as the "Three Piṭakas.
In relying upon and examining the sūtras and śāstras, it is specifically the Three Piṭakas that are pointed out as distinctively referring to the Hīnayāna.
Why rely on a single teaching? It is because when the Buddha was in the world, there were temporal sequences in his teachings, and thus there were small and great [teachings].

For example, during the twelve years at the Deer Park, while he was correctly bestowing the small teachings of the Three Vehicles, the bhikṣus merely upheld the sūtras, vinaya, and śāstras as they were spoken by the Buddha;
they did not yet know the ultimate intent of the Buddha’s meaning, even though the Buddha himself...

One cannot yet specifically designate the Tripiṭaka as the Hīnayāna; it is only when reaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Anrakugyō* (Expedient Means) that they serve as the circulating versions of the sūtras.

Furthermore, because the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains the Prajñāpāramitā as a means of refuting the Hīnayāna and establishing the Mahāyāna, one can finally specifically designate the Tripiṭaka as a single teaching of the Hīnayāna.
Thus, we know that the sūtras and śāstras of the Great Teaching specifically designate the Hīnayāna as distinct from the Tripiṭaka.

The first teaching is established to reveal that the dharmas of cause and effect within the triple world, as expounded by this teaching, are characterized by arising and ceasing, are substantially real, possess distinct differences, and are not mutually integrated.
For this reason, the four gates of this teaching are prone to many attachments and disputes. In the Tiantai system, the four teachings for transforming beings are arranged in sequence;

the names of these teachings are established with specific significations, and their meanings are interpreted according to their respective points of convergence, following each mode of transformation.
Regarding the interpretation of the meanings of the various sūtras of the five periods based on the extent of their pedagogical application, nothing can be added [to this].

I recall that during my first year of traveling to study, I initially wished to investigate the names of the teachings of the *Huayan* (Avataṃsaka) Dharma within these three piṭakas; however, I was dissatisfied and undecided.

It was only upon reading the *Qingliang Huayan Da Shu Jingqian Yimen* (The Great Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra by Qingliang, Section on the Gate of Meaning at the Beginning of the Sūtra), where the establishment of the teachings is analyzed and compared to clarify the relationship between the sūtras and the śāstras, that I finally understood it to be thus.

Living in retirement due to old age and illness, I sat in my bamboo hut for the summer retreat with nothing to do. Once again reading the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, I saw that at the very end there was mention of brushes and inkstones, showing that the author had not yet forgotten his lifelong vocation.
